'''Richard Bersohn''' (May 13, 1925 – November 18, 2003) was an American [[Chemical physics|chemical physicist]] and Higgins Professor of Natural Science at [[Columbia University]].<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |title=Bersohn, Richard, 1925-2003 |url=https://history.aip.org/phn/11410026.html |access-date=2023-10-06 |website=history.aip.org}}</ref> He was known for his research in molecular photodissociation and [[chemical kinetics]].<ref name=":1">{{Cite web |title=Richard Bersohn |url=https://pubs.aip.org/physicstoday/article/57/11/82/1016718/Richard-Bersohn |access-date=2023-10-06 |website=pubs.aip.org}}</ref>

== Early life and education ==
Bersohn was born in [[New York City]] on May 13, 1925. He grew up on [[Upper West Side]] and attended [[Hunter College High School]] and [[Horace Mann School]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Richard Bersohn, 1925-2003 |url=https://www.nasonline.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/06/bersohn-richard.pdf |access-date=October 6, 2023 |website=National Academy of Sciences}}</ref> He obtained a B.S. in chemistry from the [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]] in 1943. Shortly after graduation, he entered the [[United States Army]] and worked on the [[Manhattan Project]] at the [[Oak Ridge National Laboratory]]. Upon completing his military service, Bersohn obtained a Ph.D. from [[Harvard University]] in 1949, studying under [[John Hasbrouck Van Vleck]]. He did his thesis in [[dipole]] interactions in [[nuclear magnetic resonance]] (NMR).

== Career ==
Bersohn joined the faculty of [[Cornell University]] in 1951 as an assistant professor. He moved to [[Columbia University]] in 1959 and remained there for the rest of his career, becoming full professor in 1966 and Higgins Professor of Natural Science from 1986 to his death in 2003. He served as chair of the chemistry department from 1990 to 1996.<ref name=":0" /> 

At Columbia, Bersohn pioneered the study of [[biophysics]] and used [[Förster resonance energy transfer]] and NMR methods to study the tertiary structure of proteins. He also invented "photolysis mapping" to study the photophysical and photochemical properties of molecules. He was the first to prove that certain rotating molecules can dissociate upon interacting with light before they complete a rotation.<ref name=":2">{{Cite web |title=Obituaries |url=https://cen.acs.org/articles/82/i11/PEOPLE.html |access-date=2023-10-06 |website=Chemical & Engineering News |language=en}}</ref> His students at Columbia included [[Louis E. Brus]], a co-recipient of the 2023 [[Nobel Prize in Chemistry]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Louis E. Brus life story |url=https://www.kavliprize.org/louis-brus-autobiography |access-date=2023-10-06 |website=www.kavliprize.org}}</ref>

Bersohn was elected to the [[American Academy of Arts and Sciences]] in 1962,<ref>{{Cite web |date=2023-02-09 |title=Richard Bersohn |url=https://www.amacad.org/person/richard-bersohn |access-date=2023-10-06 |website=American Academy of Arts & Sciences |language=en}}</ref> received a [[Guggenheim Fellowship]] in 1971, and was named to the [[National Academy of Sciences]] in 1985.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Richard Bersohn |url=https://www.nasonline.org/directory-entry/richard-bersohn-9mmdvp/ |access-date=2023-10-06 |website=www.nasonline.org}}</ref> He also received the [[Herbert P. Broida Prize]] from the [[American Physical Society]]. He also held advisory positions at the [[Brookhaven National Laboratory]] and the [[National Research Council (United States)|National Research Council]] as well as an adjunct appointment at the [[Weizmann Institute of Science]].<ref name=":1" />

== Personal life ==
Bersohn died on November 18, 2003, in New York City.<ref name=":2" /><ref>{{Cite web |title=Bersohn, Richard, 1925-2003 |url=https://history.aip.org/phn/11410026.html |access-date=2023-10-06 |website=history.aip.org}}</ref> He was survived by his wife, four children, and four grandchildren.
